## 4. Deep Dive: UX Engineering & Frontend Decisions

### 4.1 Fine-Grained Reactive State (`@Observable` + `MainActor` Isolation)

First up is state management. Classic SwiftUI apps built on `ObservableObject` and `@Published` tend to invalidate whole view subtrees whenever *any* published property changes. You feel that pretty quickly as UI jank when a high-frequency control, like dragging a `SymptomSeveritySlider` or updating `symptomSyncMessage`, sits on the same screen as an expensive chart.

To avoid that, Fruitful uses Swift's **`@Observable` macro** across all three stores (`FertilityHealthStore.swift`, `NFPChartStore.swift`, `ChildProfilesStore.swift`). That lets SwiftUI track property reads at the individual field level inside `body`. Paired with `SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor`, the compiler verifies that all UI state updates stay free of data races without having to sprinkle manual `DispatchQueue.main.async` hops all over HealthKit callbacks.

### 4.2 Structured Concurrency & HealthKit Query Fan-Out

If you have worked with older HealthKit codebases, you probably remember the nested pyramids of completion-handler `HKSampleQuery` calls. Here, `FertilityHealthStore.refresh()` (`FertilityHealthStore.swift`) uses Apple's newer `HKSampleQueryDescriptor` API together with Swift **Structured Concurrency**. It fans out 7 independent reproductive queries in parallel using `async let` and commits a single atomic `FertilitySnapshot` value struct back to observable state:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant App as FruitfulApp / HomeTab
    participant HS as FertilityHealthStore (@MainActor)
    participant HK as Apple HealthKit DB
    participant NS as NFPChartStore

    User->>App: Foreground app (scenePhase == .active)
    App->>HS: await healthStore.refresh()
    par 7-Way Structured Concurrency Fan-Out (async let)
        HS->>HK: Query latest menstrualFlow (limit 1)
        HS->>HK: Query latest ovulationTestResult (limit 1)
        HS->>HK: Query latest cervicalMucusQuality (limit 1)
        HS->>HK: Query latest basalBodyTemperature (limit 1)
        HS->>HK: Query last 24 menstrualFlow (period estimator)
        HS->>HK: Query latest pregnancy (gestational week)
        HS->>HK: Query latest pregnancyTestResult (limit 1)
    end
    HK-->>HS: Concurrent HKSample results
    HS->>HS: Commit atomic FertilitySnapshot + timestamp
    HS->>HK: Load today's 8 symptom category severities
    HK-->>HS: Populate symptomSelections map

    Note over App,NS: Parallel HomeTab .task lifecycle
    App->>HS: await loadRecentNFPObservations(days: 40)
    HS->>HK: Query 40d BBT + cervicalMucus + menstrualFlow
    HK-->>HS: Samples grouped by startOfDay & converted to °F
    HS-->>App: [ImportedObservation]
    App->>NS: importHealthObservations(observations)
    NS->>NS: Merge by day, preserve manual notes/intercourse, mark .combined
```

On the write side (`saveSymptoms()` in `FertilityHealthStore.swift`), I wanted to avoid optimistic-UI drift where the screen claims something saved that actually did not. So the store batches selected severities into `[HKCategorySample]`, awaits `healthStore.save(samples)`, and immediately re-reads `symptomSelections` back from HealthKit so HealthKit stays the single source of truth.

### 4.3 Multi-Source Data Provenance & Conflict-Preserving Merge

One of the most frustrating failure modes in personal tracking apps is silently losing your own written notes whenever a wearable or OS health database syncs over the top of them. `NFPChartStore.importHealthObservations(_:)` (`NFPChartStore.swift`) prevents that through **day-normalized field-level coalescing** and an explicit **`EntrySource` provenance state machine**:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> manual: User saves AddNFPEntrySheet (no prior day record)
    [*] --> healthKit: 40-day HealthKit sync creates new day record
    [*] --> sample: User taps Load Sample Data (empty store)

    manual --> combined: HealthKit sync merges BBT/mucus/bleeding while preserving notes & intercourse
    healthKit --> combined: User opens AddNFPEntrySheet (auto-prefilled) and edits/adds notes
    sample --> combined: User edits sample day or syncs overlapping HealthKit date
    combined --> combined: Subsequent manual edit or HealthKit re-sync
```

On the UI side, `AddNFPEntrySheet` watches the selected date with `.onChange(of: date, initial: true)` (`ContentView.swift`, `prefill(from:)`) and automatically fills in existing observations whenever you pick a day you have already charted. That folds "Create" and "Edit" into a single modal with very little friction. Every row in `NFPEntryRow` then tells you plainly where the data came from (`"Manual entry"`, `"Imported from Apple Health"`, `"Apple Health + manual"`, or `"Sample data"`).

### 4.4 Data Visualization Guardrails in Swift Charts

Basal body temperature shifts are tiny, typically only **0.3°F to 0.8°F** between the follicular and luteal phases. If you leave chart scaling on autopilot, you usually end up with one of two bad outcomes: either a wide physiological range like `95–102°F` flattens the real signal into a straight line, or tight `min...max` clamping blows up `0.1°F` of thermometer noise so it looks like a fever spike.

To keep the chart honest and readable, `nfpTemperatureDomain` (`ContentView.swift`) enforces four visual guardrails:

1. **Half-degree quantization:** Observed extrema get padded by `±0.2°F` and snapped to clean `0.5°F` steps (`floor((min - 0.2) * 2) / 2` and `ceil((max + 0.2) * 2) / 2`), so the dashed gridlines (`nfpTemperatureAxisMarks`) always land on easy-to-scan half-degree ticks.
2. **Physiological clamping:** The domain stays inside `95.0...100.5°F` so a stray sensor glitch cannot blow out the viewport.
3. **Minimum visual span:** The chart requires `upperBound - lowerBound >= 1.5°F`, which stops two days of `0.1°F` noise from looking like an ovulatory shift.
4. **Redundant multivariate encoding:** A Catmull-Rom `LineMark` traces the temperature curve while overlaid `PointMark` nodes use both **color and point area** to encode the inferred `CyclePhase` (ovulation stands out at `90` pt² warm amber, menstrual days sit at `70` pt² rose, and follicular/luteal days use `60` pt² sage and forest tones).

### 4.5 Progressive Disclosure, Procedural Art & Deterministic Preview Harnesses

A few smaller interface choices ended up doing a lot of heavy lifting for the overall feel of the app:

- **Progressive-Disclosure Symptom Matrix (`symptomLoggerCard` in `ContentView.swift`):** Dumping 8 stacked sliders on someone who is pregnant and tired is a rough way to start a form. Instead, an adaptive `LazyVGrid` (`GridItem(.adaptive(minimum: 140))`) shows lightweight toggle capsules. Tapping a symptom starts it at `.mild` and reveals its discrete 4-step `SymptomSeveritySlider` (`Not present` to `Mild`, `Moderate`, and `Severe`).
- **Parametric Procedural Vector Art:** Both `TreeWithAppleIllustration` (`fertilityApp.swift`) and `TreeGrowthBadge` (`ContentView.swift`) are drawn entirely from resolution-independent SwiftUI `Shape`, `Path`, and `RadialGradient` primitives driven by a 6-stage `TreeGrowthStage` model (`trunkHeight` scaling from `46` to `94pt`, `canopySize` from `56` to `124pt`, deeper chlorophyll greens, and `1` to `6` accent leaves). There are zero raster image assets to maintain across iPhone, iPad, and visionOS screen densities.
- **Built-In Deterministic Preview Harness (`SettingsTab` in `ContentView.swift`):** Longitudinal health apps are notoriously awkward to design-review and QA because real biological states play out across 28-day cycles and 40-week pregnancies. Fruitful bakes persistent `@AppStorage` overrides right into Settings (`pregnancyPreviewWeek: 0...40` and `cyclePhasePreview: automatic | menstruation | follicular | ovulation | luteal`), along with a one-tap 14-day synthetic biphasic dataset (`seedSampleDataIfNeeded()`). That makes it straightforward to check every longitudinal UI state on demand without touching live HealthKit records.

## 5. Technical Trade-Offs & an Honest Architectural Audit

Any honest v1 build involves deliberate shortcuts. Part of doing real UX engineering and research software work is going back through your own code, naming what is rough around the edges, and spelling out how it needs to grow for v2. Auditing the source files turned up seven concrete trade-offs and bugs:

| Area | What v1 Does Today | Why I Built It That Way | Known Trade-Offs & Code-Level Findings | Concrete v2 Fix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Persistence & Privacy** | Apple HealthKit plus `UserDefaults` JSON blobs (`nfpChartEntries`, `childProfiles`), with no cloud backend. | Full on-device data ownership, zero server attack surface, fast early iteration, and zero external dependencies. | `UserDefaults` re-encodes the entire array on every change (`O(n)` write amplification), has no relational indexing or schema migration path, and offers no user-controlled backup or export. | Move local stores to **SwiftData / SQLite** with a versioned `SchemaMigrationPlan`, optional end-to-end encrypted CloudKit sync, and portable **CSV / JSON-LD / FHIR** export. |
| **2. Canonical Domain Engine & Unit Consistency** | Phase inference is split between `makeCyclePhaseInfo` in the view layer and `NFPChartStore.phase(for:)`; BBT formats in `°C` in `FertilityHealthStore` and `°F` in `NFPChartStore`. | Fast parallel prototyping of HealthKit dashboard cards alongside the standalone NFP chart. | **Two real bugs showed up in the audit:** (a) mixed `°C` and `°F` units between `FertilityHealthStore.swift` L398–399 and `NFPChartStore.swift` L241; (b) `makeCyclePhaseVisualState` (`ContentView.swift`) checks `.contains("menstruation")` while live inference returns `"Menstrual phase"` (L201), which makes live menstrual snapshots fall back visually to `.follicular`. | Pull this into a single, unit-tested **`CycleDomainEngine`** using strongly typed enums (no string matching on display labels) and `Measurement<UnitTemperature>` formatted with `Locale.current`. |

On top of that, 8 sequential symptom queries add avoidable IPC latency. | Have `loadLatestPregnancy()` return a pure `(summary: String, week: Int?)` tuple; parallelize the 8 symptom queries with `withThrowingTaskGroup` and the 3 NFP queries with `async let`. |
| **4. Sympto-Thermal Clinical Fidelity vs. Transparency** | Deterministic `+0.3°F` jump over a 6-day mean (`>=3` prior temps), with cycle start anchored to `entries.last(where: heavy \|\| medium)`. | Inspectable, transparent heuristic that avoids black-box ML predictions and sticks to non-diagnostic wording. | `entries.last(where:)` (`NFPChartStore.swift`) anchors Cycle Day 1 to the *last* bleeding day rather than the *first* day of the current menstrual block. ## 6. Where This Connects to Digital Humanities & Academic Research

Outside of commercial frontend engineering, a lot of Fruitful's design maps directly onto methods in **Digital Humanities (DH)**, **Health and Medical Humanities**, **Science and Technology Studies (STS)**, and **Human-Centered Research Software Engineering (RSE)**:

### 1. Critical Making & Values-Sensitive Design (VSD)
For those who have spent time with Friedman and Hendry's *Value Sensitive Design* or D'Ignazio and Klein's *Data Feminism*, the core premise is familiar: software interfaces are never neutral pipes. Every layout and database schema encodes cultural and ethical commitments, whether the author admits it or not. Instead of burying its worldview under sterile clinical minimalism or engagement-driven growth hooks, Fruitful puts its stance right out in the open (*Genesis 1:28*, hospitality toward family life, and complete user ownership of intimate records) in both its visual language and its zero-cloud architecture. It is a practical exercise in translating humanistic inquiry into working software decisions.

### 2. Data Provenance as a Visible Interface Element
In archival studies, digital editions (TEI/XML), and linked humanities data (CIDOC-CRM, W3C PROV-O), keeping track of the difference between a primary observation, a machine-imported record, a merged synthesis, and an illustrative sample is basic scholarly hygiene. Fruitful brings that exact habit into a consumer health app, both in the data model (`EntrySource`: `.manual`, `.healthKit`, `.combined`, `.sample`) and directly in the UI (`NFPEntryRow` provenance captions). It is a good reminder that humanities data-modeling discipline makes everyday consumer and clinical tools clearer and more trustworthy.

### 3. Affective, Metaphorical & Longitudinal Visualization
Numbers on a time-series chart only tell part of a human story. Fruitful pairs **analytical visualization** (precision Catmull-Rom BBT curves with strict half-degree domain guardrails) alongside **metaphorical and biographical visualization** (gestational fruit scales, phase-modulated peach icons, and procedurally growing trees matched with developmental prose). That dual-register approach translates naturally to DH projects in **narrative medicine, oral history, biographical timelines, and public-facing cultural heritage exhibits**.

### 4. IRB-Safe Prototyping & Reproducible Walkthroughs
Academic UX and participatory design researchers run into the same ethical snag all the time: how do you review a sensitive health or biographical interface with faculty collaborators, peer reviewers, or an IRB board without exposing real participant PHI? Fruitful's **deterministic Settings preview harnesses** (`CyclePhasePreview`, `pregnancyPreviewWeek`) and **synthetic biphasic dataset** (`seedSampleDataIfNeeded()`) double as a built-in research demo kit. Anyone can step through every state reproducibly for peer review, usability workshops, or classroom teaching without putting a single real person's data at risk.

### 5. A Pattern for Consent-First Participatory Health Tools
More broadly, this zero-backend, HealthKit-backed setup works well as a **reusable RSE reference pattern for university health-humanities and community-based participatory research (CBPR)**:
- Participants keep 100% custody of their sensitive biometric and qualitative diary records on their own devices.
- Studies can layer an explicit, revocable, locally anonymized export step (such as a JSON-LD or REDCap-compatible bundle) only at the exact moment of informed consent, cutting institutional security liability while giving participants real reasons to trust the tool.

Even at v1, though, building Fruitful confirmed something I have believed for a long time: you do not have to choose between serious engineering craft and software that treats human life with quiet respect.
